title: The Devil Made Them Do It, Or So We're Told; Life In Hell Has Never Looked

contact_edits.before: Probably, given enough time, any three people could torment each other as effectively, but the devils at the end of the phone seem to want quick results. It does mean though that, dramatically speaking, there is something arbitrary about the whole set-up, reinforced by Sartre's inability to bring his dead characters to life. There's nothing especially compelling about their earthly biographies, or about how they're revealed to us, and the ways in which they torture one another are surprisingly limited. But if the play can't develop its conception, except to a pre-ordained philosophic conclusion, the conception itself is genius. And it's in illustrating it, drilling into it, that Collier's production is at its strongest. We are watching the actors, most of the time, in giant unforgiving close-up, and they respond with performances that are ingrained and unflinching. Andy Thompson's vulpine Cradeau tends to generalize, but the women are fiercely specific, Laara Sadiq's bruised incisiveness as Inez balancing the elegant meltdown of Lucia Frangione's Estelle. The triple screen isolates them, and accentuates the moments when one crosses into another's territory. Just occasionally an aerial surveillance shot shows us the whole room, an oppressively ornate Second Empire chamber, with heavy ornaments that can't be lifted and a door that mostly won't open (and when it does, doesn't lead anywhere you'd dare to go). Hell is also other furniture; and the sight of the three of them marooned there is far more powerful than in the sustained long-shot of a conventional staging. See them in hell. - No Exit closes tonight at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre. For ticket information, call 416-955-0101.
